_meta.note: Original Waystead stories, one per curriculum chapter. A story reaches children only once `reviewed` is true here: set it with tools/approve-stories.mjs, never by hand. tests/stories.test.js checks length and that every chapter word is used.

stories.title: The Queen of the Compost Heap
sentences: Class Four had a garden behind the hall, and every group had its own patch of earth.
Nell's group wanted to build a shelter for hedgehogs.
They measured the length of the fence with a ball of string, then stacked up logs and leaves.
"We need to learn what hedgehogs like to eat," said Asha.
"Not much fruit," said Tom, who had read a whole book about them.
That evening, as the sun went down, they heard a snuffling noise behind the compost heap.
Nell held her breath, and her heart went thump, thump, thump.
Out came a small round hedgehog, walking as if she owned the place.
"She's our queen," Asha whispered.
"Long may she reign!"
All autumn, the children took turns to stand guard by the shelter door, although the queen mostly just snored.
When spring came she woke up, blinked at them all, and trotted off to inspect her kingdom.

stories.title: The Walking Club
sentences: Mrs Okoro was a busy woman who ran the Saturday walking club.
She was often the first one up, and she met everyone early at the town centre.
"Today," she said, "I am your guide, and we are walking in a giant circle round the lake."
Two women from the bakery came along, and so did Idris, who was eight and wanted to prove his strength.
By noon his legs felt like jelly.
"How far is it now?" he asked.
Mrs Okoro smiled.
"Do you want the kind answer or the actual answer?"
"The kind one, please."
"Nearly there," she said, and handed him a toffee.
The actual answer was three more miles, but the toffee helped, and so did the two women, who sang silly songs the whole way.
When they reached the town again, Idris was tired, muddy and very pleased with himself.

stories.title: The Island That Moved
sentences: The boat rocked strangely as Mei and her uncle rowed forward through the mist.
"That's odd," said Uncle Jun.
"There's no island on this map, and it's quite a recent map."
Yet a low green island seemed to appear in front of them, about a quarter of a mile away.
Mei was certain it had not been there at breakfast.
"Row straight for it," she said.
They rowed forwards a little more, and the strange island let out a long, slow sigh.
Mei could hardly breathe.
A huge wet eye opened and looked at her kindly.
It was no island at all, but a great old whale, covered in green weed.
It rolled gently, sent a fountain of spray into the sky and sank away without a sound.
Mei and Uncle Jun told the story on the harbour wall that night.
Nobody believed them, but the tale soon became famous all along the coast.

stories.title: Grandad's Bicycle
sentences: In the shed there was a bicycle nearly a century old.
Grandad said it had a long history.
It had carried bread, letters and various cross little dogs.
"I've decided," said Ravi.
"I am going to mend it."
He wrote a list, though his grammar made his sister laugh.
It took eight weekends to clean the rusty wheels, and each one felt like it went past in a minute.
On the final Sunday, Ravi wheeled it out and rang the bell.
"I can't believe it!" Grandad said.
"You didn't even notice the rain!"
Ravi hadn't.
He had been too busy to look up.
"Well, you must decide who rides it first."
Ravi held out the handlebars.
Grandad wobbled, laughed and rode to the end of the lane with extreme care.
He came back pink in the face and looking about ten years younger.
"Best ride of the century," he said.

stories.title: The Book That Came Back
sentences: A very special book came back to the library one wet Tuesday.
It had no address on the parcel, only a note.
"Sorry this is late," it said.
"I promise I can explain."
Miss Lund looked at the date inside.
The book was sixty years overdue!
"Perhaps we should mention it in the newsletter," she said to Priya, who was a regular visitor.
It was a natural history of British birds, and it had once been the most popular book on the shelf.
Priya opened it, and a pressed feather slid out and was caught by the draught.
Under the feather was a second note, written in careful pencil.
"I kept it for a purpose," it said.
"Every bird in here, I went out and found."
Miss Lund smiled and put the book back on its shelf.
There was no fine to pay.
Sixty years of birdwatching seemed like a very good reason to be late.

stories.title: The Eighth Pumpkin
sentences: On the calendar in the kitchen, a red ring marked the day of the pumpkin show.
Ollie had grown seven small pumpkins, though none of them was any good.
The eighth pumpkin was different.
It had grown to the height of his knee, and he could not lift its weight on his own.
"Consider this," said Dad.
"If we use the wheelbarrow, we can arrive before the judges do."
So they set off.
They had to stop twice and continue slowly up the hill, but at last the job was complete.
A lady with a clipboard asked Ollie to describe how he had grown it.
"I talked to it," he said.
"I told it about my day."
The judges laughed, and they gave him first prize.
It was the only thing Ollie had ever wanted to possess: a small green rosette, which he stuck on the kitchen wall.

stories.title: The Potato Surprise
sentences: It was the coldest day in February, and Class Three were getting ready for a surprise.
Mr Bell had an interest in peculiar experiments, so nobody was shocked when he brought in a sack of potatoes.
"Remember what we thought about electricity?" he asked.
"Probably not," said Zainab, which made him chuckle.
He pushed two strips of metal into a potato and joined them with a wire.
Then he added more potatoes, one by one, to increase the power.
Nobody thought it would work, but a tiny light began to glow.
"Potatoes!" gasped Zainab.
"It isn't magic," said Mr Bell.
"The material inside the potato helps the power move along the wire."
For homework, everyone had to write one sentence about what they had seen.
Zainab wrote, "Never be rude to a potato."
Mr Bell gave her a gold star for that, and he had a jacket potato for his lunch.

stories.title: The Lemonade Business
sentences: Ana and Finn had an important idea.
"Suppose we open a business," said Ana.
"We could sell lemonade to the people going through the park."
It was difficult at first.
A wasp made one customer disappear in a hurry, and there was a small accident with a jug.
Finn could feel the pressure.
"Imagine if nobody comes," he said.
"Let's try something different," said Ana.
She wrote a new sign in huge letters: "Lemonade: Actually Quite Nice."
A man laughed and bought two cups.
Then a whole football team came by and bought the lot.
By teatime the jug was empty and the money tin was heavy.
"What shall we do with it?" asked Finn.
They counted it twice, then walked to the animal shelter and dropped it all in the collection box.
"Same again next week?" said Ana.
Finn looked at the sticky table and grinned.

stories.title: A Naughty Pony
sentences: Pepper was the naughty pony at Hill Farm.
She was no ordinary pony.
She could undo gates, and she had a good knowledge of where the carrots were kept.
"That's enough, Pepper," said Lucy, who looked after her every morning.
Then one day Pepper would not eat, not even her favourite apple.
The vet took her temperature and asked Lucy question after question.
"She needs some medicine, and a stable of her own," said the vet.
"Keep her separate from the others, and no exercise for a week."
Therefore Lucy sat with her every day after school, in the same position on an upturned bucket, reading out loud.
Pepper seemed to like the stories.
On the seventh day, Lucy heard a clink behind her.
Pepper had undone the stable gate.
"You're better!" laughed Lucy, and she gave her the biggest apple she could find.

stories.title: The Great Bean Experiment
sentences: Although Kit had never grown anything, she signed up for the science club's big experiment.
Each child had to plant two beans in two particular places.
One sat on the sunny windowsill, and the other in the dark cupboard on the opposite side of the room.
"Is it possible they will both grow?" asked Kit.
"Let's find out," said Dr Shah.
Kit watered them occasionally, then every day, as she gained more experience.
On one occasion she accidentally knocked the windowsill pot to the floor and had to scoop up the soil with a spoon.
That bean was her proudest possession, and she was terribly worried.
Yet it grew green and strong.
The cupboard bean grew too, but it was pale and thin, stretching towards the crack of light under the door.
"Plants don't give up," said Dr Shah, "and neither did you."
Even now, Kit occasionally checks on it, just to say hello.

stories.title: The Yacht Race
sentences: At the regatta, the queue for the small boats stretched along the whole harbour wall.
Forty children were waiting, and Sana felt awkward in her borrowed life jacket.
Her uncle's little yacht had a symbol of a blue fish on its sail.
"We have a system," he said.
"Pull, tie, duck."
They had even made up a rhyme to help her remember it.
Pull the rope, tie it tight, duck the boom and you'll be right.
Soon Sana found the rhythm of it, and every muscle in her arms began to ache in a satisfying way.
The boom caught her elbow on the second turn, which left a purple bruise.
She did not mind.
They crossed the line in third place, and she hopped ashore grinning.
"Same time next year?" said her uncle.
Sana showed off her bruise to anyone who would look at it.
"Pull, tie, duck," she said.
"Definitely."

stories.title: The Soldier's Letter
sentences: Dara's neighbour, Mr Novak, spent his leisure hours mending old clocks.
One stormy evening, a flash of lightning made the lights go out, and Dara took a candle round to check on him.
He was holding a yellowed letter written in a foreign language.
"My grandfather was a soldier," he said.
"He wrote this on the twelfth of March, long ago, and I have never read it."
Dara was conscious of how much it mattered.
She felt a flutter in her stomach.
"We could find out what it says," she said.
It took a thorough search of the library, and three weeks with a dictionary, but they did it.
The letter was not about battles.
It said, "Tell my son I am sorry I missed his birthday."
Mr Novak was quiet for a long time.
"He had a good conscience," he said at last, and he put the letter inside his best clock.

stories.title: The Seagull Committee
sentences: According to the sign, the seafront café could accommodate thirty people.
On Saturday it had to accommodate one aggressive seagull too.
The bird would occupy a table, stare at the customers and harass anyone who had chips.
It was starting to embarrass the owner, Mrs Doyle.
"It's necessary to do something," she said, and she formed a committee.
Her son and two friends offered to accompany her to the beach to study the problem.
"These things only occur when the bird is hungry," said Theo.
So the committee built a feeding table at the far end of the pier, and put out scraps each morning.
It worked.
By the end of the month, the seagull was too full to bother anyone.
Now it sits on the pier like a small, fat king.
Customers bring their cameras, and Mrs Doyle has put its picture on the menu.

stories.title: The Treehouse Radio
sentences: Jude and Amara wanted to communicate from one end of the street to the other.
"I suggest a radio," said Amara.
Jude's aunt, who repaired old equipment, offered to equip them with two battered handsets.
Each one had a long wire attached to the back.
"I don't want to exaggerate," she said, "but these are the finest radios in town."
The children appreciate a challenge, and they soon had the treehouse fully equipped.
Then the crackling started.
"Do not interfere with the dial," said Jude.
"I'm not!" said Amara.
"Sorry to interrupt," said a third voice.
They both froze.
"Who's that?"
"It's Mr Wells at number nine.
I can hear you on my radio.
Would you like to know what the weather is doing?"
From then on, every evening at six, Mr Wells read them the weather, and they told him all the news of the street.

stories.title: The Ancient Coin
sentences: It was hardly a convenience to have a metal detector that beeped frequently at bottle tops.
For Leo's mother it was a nuisance, and for Leo's patience it was a hindrance.
"Do you have sufficient evidence of treasure yet?" she asked.
Leo shook his head.
Then, at the far end of the field, the beeping changed.
He dug carefully until the apparent lump of mud came away in his hand.
It was a coin, small and thin and very ancient.
The museum said it was an excellent find.
"This proves the existence of a Roman road here," said the curator, who was thrilled.
It was relevant to everything they had been trying to learn about the valley.
Leo's name went on the little card in the display case.
His mother read it three times.
"I take it all back," she said.
"Beep as much as you like."

stories.title: The Cake Competition
sentences: The village baking competition was only days away, and Hana was desperate to enter.
She had one definite problem: her cake sank in the middle every time.
"I hate to criticise," said her brother, "but it looks like a crater."
She needed an immediate solution.
So she made a great sacrifice and gave up her Saturday to practise.
Her neighbour, a retired chef, gave her an explanation of what was going wrong.
"You keep opening the oven," he said.
"And it's called a génoise, by the way."
Hana's pronunciation made him smile.
On the day, she did not open the oven door once.
When the judges arrived, they could immediately recognise that this cake was something special.
It was tall and golden and perfectly level.
She won second place, and her brother ate three slices.
"It still looks a bit like a crater," he said, reaching for a fourth.

stories.title: The Food Van
sentences: Bea's dad was an amateur cook with a big dream: a restaurant on wheels.
He bought an old vehicle and painted it yellow, and Bea, who liked lists, became his secretary.
There was some controversy over the name.
"The Soup Wagon," said Dad.
"The Ladle of Destiny," said Bea, who had looked up clever words in the dictionary.
They parked by the gate of the old cemetery, where walkers came to admire the wild daffodils.
It was hard physical work, chopping and stirring all morning.
On the first day, a lady spoke to them in a language they did not know, then pointed hopefully at the soup.
Dad gave her a bowl and she beamed.
At the end of the year, the van won a prize in the category of Best Newcomer.
"The Soup Wagon," said the certificate.
Bea sighed, smiled and put the certificate in a very neat file.

stories.title: The Lost Tortoise
sentences: It was no average Monday when Max found a tortoise asleep under his school bag.
He swung the bag over his shoulder and knelt down with growing curiosity.
It seemed familiar.
There was a tiny signature painted on its shell: Tilly.
That was the name of the tortoise from the school environment club!
The temperature was dropping, and Max knew tortoises hate the cold.
He had to persuade his friends to help.
"We can achieve this," he said.
"We just need a plan."
They began to develop one straight away.
Sam found a box, Nia found some lettuce, and together they carried Tilly back across the field.
Mrs Grant, the club leader, was almost in tears.
"We've been looking for two days!"
Max's name went up on the club's board, and the gap in the fence was mended that afternoon.
Tilly chewed her lettuce slowly, as if nothing at all had happened.

stories.title: The Mischievous Goat
sentences: Every individual in the community had an opinion about Gerald.
Gerald was a marvellous goat, but a mischievous one.
He had eaten the programme at the summer fair and most of the mayor's speech.
The school had its own small parliament, and Year Six formed a government for one week as a project.
Their first opportunity to pass a law came quickly.
"I can guarantee he'll eat the bunting next," said Rosa, who wanted to go into the legal profession.
The class voted on what to do.
Some wanted a taller fence.
Rosa had a better idea.
"Give him a job," she said.
So Gerald was put in charge of the long grass by the playing field, and within a month it was as neat as a carpet.
The school saved money on the mower.
Gerald, for his part, got to eat as much as he liked, and nobody's speech was ever in danger again.

stories.title: The Vegetable Stall
sentences: Mina's family ran a vegetable stall, and the market was the place for a bargain.
A wide variety of marrows sat on the table, available at a very fair price.
Mina was determined to sell them all, especially the enormous one.
Sadly, the first attempt was disastrous, because nobody liked marrows.
There was a real prejudice against them.
"Tell people a recipe," said her grandmother.
"I recommend marrow and ginger jam."
Mina had a pen friend in Wales with whom she would correspond, and she wrote to ask for ideas.
A week later she had a whole new identity for the stall: The Marrow Jam Company.
It was a sincere effort, and people could taste that.
"It has been a privilege," said an old man, buying his third jar.
Mina wrote to her friend that evening.
"Thank you for the idea," she wrote.
"Yours sincerely, the Queen of Marrows."
